q: Hypoglycaemia in an infant of a diabetic mother is due to:
e: Fetal hyperinsulinism continues after maternal glucose stops.

q: The most specific congenital anomaly in an infant of a diabetic mother is:
e: Caudal regression is rare but most specific to maternal diabetes.

q: All are complications of an infant of a diabetic mother EXCEPT:
A jittery IDM has glucose 1.8 mmol/L and a seizure. Treatment is:
e: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia: IV 10% glucose bolus, then 60–90 ml/kg/day.

q: A well IDM has glucose 2.3 mmol/L at 3 hours and is feeding. The best step is:
o: Feed and give 40% dextrose gel, then recheck
e: Asymptomatic: feed + buccal dextrose gel 0.5 ml/kg, recheck in 30–60 min.

q: Late neonatal hypocalcaemia (end of the first week) is classically caused by:
Neonatal polycythaemia is defined as a venous haematocrit above:
e: > 65%; symptomatic babies need partial exchange with saline.

q: A breastfed baby born at home without vitamin K has melaena on day 3; platelets are normal and PT is long. Diagnosis?
e: Classic VKDB: day 2–7, no prophylaxis, breast milk low in vitamin K.

q: Treatment of vitamin K deficiency bleeding is:
o: Vitamin K 1 mg IV (+ FFP if serious)
e: Vitamin K corrects the factors within hours; FFP for serious bleeding.

q: A well newborn vomits blood. The test to show it is maternal blood is:
e: Fetal Hb resists alkali and stays pink; maternal Hb turns brown.
